subsection: 4. Adapting to external drivers through the marketing mix and business model

notes.b: External drivers are changes outside the business that force it to adapt. STEEPLE is a checklist for finding them, and the aim of adapting is to keep the business financially sustainable.
points: Customer demographics, such as an ageing population or a rise in single-person households, change what customers buy and how they buy.
Competition, including new entrants and substitutes, changes the prices and features a business needs to match.
Economic factors, such as inflation, interest rates and consumer incomes, change both costs and customers' spending power.
Technological, legal and environmental drivers, such as new digital channels, a rise in the minimum wage or stricter packaging rules, change costs and customer expectations.
A business that adapts early keeps its revenue and cost structure under control, while one that waits may be forced into deep cuts.

notes.b: The product or service is the first lever, and changes here affect what customers see and what it costs to provide.
points: Changing the range to meet demand, such as a restaurant adding plant-based dishes as customer preferences shift.
Adjusting the offer for a customer group, such as smaller portions for older customers with smaller appetites.
Dropping low-selling or high-cost lines to protect margin when input costs rise.

notes.b: Price changes need care, because a rise that customers reject can lose more sales than it gains.
points: Passing on cost rises through price increases works only if customers still see the offer as good value.
Value packs and bundles keep customers buying when household budgets tighten.
Loyalty discounts or subscriptions give a regular price in return for commitment from the customer.

notes.b: Promotion should follow the channels customers actually use as their habits change.
points: Moving spending from print to digital channels, such as social media or email, when customers change how they find products.
Reaching older customers through channels they use, such as local newspapers or community noticeboards, rather than online adverts alone.
Using loyalty schemes and personal offers to keep existing customers when a competitor opens nearby.

notes.b: Staffing and operations often offset rising costs, but they must be managed with care.
points: People: retraining staff or hiring for new skills, such as online order handling, so the workforce matches new demands.
People: flexible rosters or part-time contracts help manage wage costs when labour costs rise, though they can affect staff morale.
Process: self-ordering screens or app-based ordering reduce the staff needed per sale, which offsets part of a higher wage bill.
Process: tighter stock control cuts waste and cost without changing what the customer receives.

notes.b: Packaging and place decide how the product reaches customers and how it is presented.
points: Packaging: eco-friendly materials respond to sustainability goals, and smaller or resealable packs suit single-person households.
Place: online ordering, delivery or click-and-collect extends the business's reach beyond its premises.
Place: opening in a town where the population is growing follows demographic change, rather than waiting for the local market to shrink.

notes.b: The business model is the widest response. It changes how the business earns money and what it does itself.
points: New revenue streams, such as catering, merchandise or meal kits, add income that does not depend on the core product alone.
New channels, such as a listing on a marketplace or a delivery partnership, widen the route to customers.
A subscription model turns some one-off sales into regular payments, which makes income easier to forecast.
Outsourcing non-core activities, such as payroll, delivery or cleaning, turns some fixed costs into variable payments and frees managers' time.

notes.h: Worked example: rising labour costs in a restaurant
notes.b: A restaurant facing a rise in the minimum wage can combine several adaptations rather than rely on one.
points: The direct effect is higher labour costs, which squeeze the margin if prices and staffing stay the same.
Pricing: a modest price rise on main dishes, with a value lunch option kept, passes on part of the cost while protecting the price-sensitive lunchtime trade.
Process: tablet ordering at tables reduces the number of staff needed to take orders, which offsets part of the wage rise.
Product: a shorter menu built on shared ingredients cuts waste and speeds up service in the kitchen.
Business model: a weekly meal subscription for local office workers adds regular income to quieter weekday periods.
Evaluation: the changes take time to set up and may not fully offset the cost, so the owner should track margins after each one.

notes.h: Worked example: an ageing population in a town
notes.b: A café in a town whose population is ageing adapts several parts of the marketing mix together.
points: Product: smaller portions, softer foods and a quieter seating area suit older customers.
Place: step-free access and accessible toilets make the café easier to use.
Promotion: flyers in community centres and local radio reach older customers who may not use social media.
Business model: a morning coffee club with a fixed monthly fee gives regular, predictable income.

notes.h: Challenges of launching a new product
notes.b: Introducing a new product carries risks that the business should plan for before launch.
points: Low customer awareness can be tackled with a launch promotion and free samples.
High development and launch costs can be managed with a phased launch in one region before a wider roll-out.
Cannibalisation, where the new product takes sales from an existing line, can be limited by positioning it at a different customer group or price point.
Supply problems can be reduced by agreeing supplier capacity with key partners before the launch.

questions.prompt: A small Irish bookshop faces rising rents and a shift of customers to online shopping. Explain how it could adapt its marketing mix and business model to protect its financial sustainability.
questions.model: Product: stock more gift and local-interest titles and run author events, which are harder to replicate online. Price: offer a loyalty card or a paid membership with discounts, which builds repeat custom. Place: add an online store with click-and-collect, so the shop's premises are used for both browsing and collection. Business model: add new revenue streams such as café sales or paid workshops, and outsource online order delivery to a courier to avoid fixed delivery costs. Financial sustainability is the aim, so each change should be tested against its cost and cash flow before the bookshop commits to it.

questions.prompt: A business plans to launch a new product that may take sales from its existing range. Explain two challenges this creates and how the business could address them.
questions.model: The first challenge is cannibalisation, where the new product takes sales from existing lines and lowers overall margin. The business can address it by positioning the new product at a different customer group or price point, so the range widens rather than simply replacing sales. The second challenge is the high development and launch cost, which strains cash. The business can reduce the risk with a phased launch in one region first, measuring sales before a national roll-out.
